content: Thalassaemia is a genetic disorder characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis, leading to chronic anemia. Individuals with thalassaemia major often require regular red blood cell transfusions, which result in secondary iron overload. This iron overload can lead to severe complications if left untreated, necessitating the use of iron chelation therapy. Historically, deferoxamine and deferiprone have been effective treatments for managing iron overload. However, the newer oral iron chelator, deferasirox, requires a thorough evaluation of its efficacy and safety in this population. A systematic review was conducted to assess the effectiveness and safety of deferasirox in individuals with thalassaemia and iron overload. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing deferasirox to placebo, no therapy, or other iron chelators. Sixteen studies involving 1,807 participants were analyzed. These studies included comparisons of deferasirox to placebo, deferoxamine, deferiprone, and combinations of these chelators. Two studies (47 participants) compared deferasirox to placebo in individuals with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia. These studies demonstrated that deferasirox effectively promoted net iron excretion. The safety profile was acceptable, warranting further investigation in phase II and III trials. Nine studies (1,251 participants) compared deferasirox to deferoxamine. The data suggested that deferasirox could achieve similar efficacy to deferoxamine, depending on the dosing ratio. In a phase III study, comparable or superior efficacy in reducing serum ferritin and liver iron concentration (LIC) was observed in individuals with high iron overload when deferasirox was administered at a mean dose of 28.2 mg/day compared to deferoxamine at 51.6 mg/day (a ratio of 1 mg deferasirox to 1.8 mg deferoxamine). The pooled analysis showed moderate-quality evidence for reductions in serum ferritin (mean difference [MD] 454.42 ng/mL, 95% confidence interval [CI] 337.13 to 571.71) and LIC (MD 2.37 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.07). However, there was substantial heterogeneity in the results, likely due to variations in dosing ratios. Data on mortality and safety at the required doses for effective chelation were limited. Patient satisfaction was higher with deferasirox compared to deferoxamine (risk ratio [RR] 2.20, 95% CI 1.89 to 2.57), and the rate of treatment discontinuation was similar for both drugs. Four studies (205 participants) compared deferasirox to deferiprone. One study (41 participants) reported a higher incidence of arthralgia in the deferiprone group, but the overall results were inconclusive due to the wide range of adverse events reported. Another study (96 participants) compared the combination of deferasirox and deferiprone to deferiprone with deferoxamine. Participants receiving the combination of oral chelators demonstrated better adherence, and no participants discontinued the study. In comparisons involving deferasirox and deferiprone, or deferasirox and deferoxamine, only a limited number of patient-relevant outcomes were reported, and no significant differences were observed. One study (166 participants) evaluated deferasirox in individuals with non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, comparing two different doses of deferasirox to placebo. Deferasirox significantly reduced serum ferritin (MD -306.74 ng/mL, 95% CI -398.23 to -215.24) and LIC (MD -3.27 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI -4.44 to -2.09). The incidence of adverse events and treatment discontinuation was similar between the deferasirox and placebo groups. No deaths were reported, but the follow-up period was limited to one year. In conclusion, deferasirox represents an important treatment option for individuals with thalassaemia and secondary iron overload. While it does not appear to be superior to deferoxamine at the commonly recommended dosing ratio of 1 mg deferasirox to 2 mg deferoxamine, similar efficacy can be achieved depending on the dose and ratio. Long-term benefits comparable to those of deferoxamine remain to be confirmed. Data on rare toxicities and long-term safety are limited. However, deferasirox may be considered a first-line treatment for individuals who prefer it or for those who experience intolerance or poor adherence to deferoxamine, following a detailed discussion of the potential risks and benefits.
